title: Subgroups and the center
terms: subgroup; proper subgroup; trivial subgroup; subgroup test; center of a group.

exposition.text:
A subgroup H ≤ G is a subset that is a group under the same operation. The efficient sub-
−1
group test is: H is nonempty and ab ∈ H for all a, b ∈ H. A proper subgroup is different
from G, and the trivial subgroup is {e}. For finite nonempty subsets, closure under multiplica-
tion alone suffices.
The center Z(G) = {z : zg = gz for all g ∈ G} is an Abelian subgroup, and in fact normal.
Intersections of subgroups are subgroups, but unions need not be: H ∪ K is a subgroup exactly
when one of H, K contains the other. The trivial group has only one subgroup, so the usual two
examples need not be distinct.
For finite subgroups, the product set HK = {hk : h ∈ H, k ∈ K} has cardinality |H||K|/|H ∩
K|, even when HK is not itself a subgroup. This gives intersection bounds. A union of three
proper subgroups can be a whole group, as in V , despite the restriction on unions of two. In
4
the quotient notation used below, G/Z(G) identifies elements differing by a central factor.

question.text:
Which group is the union of three proper subgroups?
(A) Z
4
(B) Z
6
(C) Z
8
(D) The Klein four-group V
4
(E) Z
9

solution.text:
The three subgroups of order two in V each contain the identity and one different non-
4
identity element, so their union is all of V . A cyclic group cannot be covered by proper
4
subgroups, since a generator belongs to none of them. The theorem about a union of two
subgroups does not extend to a union of three.

question.text:
For n ≥ 2, which matrices comprise the center of GL(n, R)?
(A) All diagonal invertible matrices
(B) All determinant-one matrices
(C) All nonzero scalar matrices
(D) Only the identity matrix
(E) All symmetric invertible matrices

solution.text:
Commuting with every diagonal invertible matrix forces all off-diagonal entries to van-
ish. Commuting with every permutation matrix then forces all diagonal entries to agree.
Conversely, every nonzero scalar matrix commutes with every matrix.

question.text:
If H, K are subgroups of orders 12, 18 in a group of order 36, what is the least possible order of
H ∩ K?
(A) 6 (B) 3 (C) 2 (D) 1 (E) 12

solution.text:
The set HK has size |H||K|/|H ∩ K| ≤ 36, forcing intersection size at least six. In a cyclic
group of order 36, the subgroups of orders 12, 18 intersect in the subgroup of order six.

question.text:
If G/Z(G) is cyclic, which must be true?
(A) G is finite (B) G is abelian (C) |G| is prime (D) Z(G) = {e} (E) G is cyclic

solution.text:
a b
Writing elements as g z and g w with z, w central shows that they commute. Thus G =
Z(G), although an abelian group need not be cyclic.

question.text:
For a subgroup H ≤ G, which condition is sufficient for H to be normal?
(A) G is finite (B) H is abelian (C) |H| = 2 (D) [G : H] = 2 (E) H is cyclic

solution.text:
With index two there is only one coset other than H, so the nontrivial left and right cosets
both equal G \ H. Therefore all left and right cosets agree.

Which subsets of the multiplicative group R must be subgroups? (I) {x : x ∈ Q}; (II) {x :
|x| ≥ 1}; (III) any finite nonempty subset closed under multiplication.
(A) I only (B) II only (C) I and III only (D) II and III only (E) I, II, and III

solution.text:
−1 2 2 2
I contains one, and (xy ) = x /y remains rational, so the subgroup test applies. II
contains two but omits its inverse 1/2. For III, left multiplication by any member permutes
the finite subset, since ambient cancellation makes it injective. Surjectivity first forces the
identity into the subset and then supplies each inverse. This proves III without assuming
those properties at the start.
